newsitem.title: FINLAND: Markka seen stable ahead Oct-Nov ERM entry - report.
newsitem.headline: Markka seen stable ahead Oct-Nov ERM entry - report.

text.p: The Finnish markka is expected to remain stable ahead of a likely decision in October-November to link it to Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM), according to a report in Euromoney magazine received on Wednesday.

"The currency can be expected to remain stable and strong against the background of low inflation, a healthy current account, improving public finances and the looming ERM and EMU membership," Swedish bank Handelsbanken Markets wrote in the report published in a World Economic Analysis supplement to Euromoney's annual IMF/World Bank issue.

"The probability of fixing the markka to the ERM rises sharply in late October and November," it said, adding Finland's pro-EMU government "will link the markka to the ERM and make every effort towards gaining EMU membership."
Finland has repeatedly said it aims to be in the first group of countries entering the third phase of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
"Even the fact that Sweden is not likely to join from the beginning does not pose a threat for the Finnish membership," Handelsbanken Markets said.
Finnish macro-economic prospects were bright, it said.
Describing the economy as being on a "stable growth path," the bank forecast Finnish 1996 GDP growth at two percent and 1997 growth at 3.2 percent.

"The current account showed a surplus of 24 billion markka in 1995 and is forecast to record a healthy surplus of 3.5 percent of GDP this year and next, effectively wiping out the external debt," it said.
At the end of July, Finnish net foreign debt was 235.8 billion markka. It was 233.3 billion at the end of 1995.

Tight fiscal policy and stable import prices augured well for inflation, which Handelsbanken put at just below one percent in 1996. "Next year, inflation is bound to accelerate but should not exceed the two-percent threshold set by the Bank of Finland," it said.
With August CPI up 0.4 percent year-on-year compared to 0.5 percent in July, Finnish inflation is the slowest in Europe.
As a result of the tight fiscal policy adopted by the current government from the previous regime, Finnish public sector debt to GDP would fall below two percent in 1997, Handelsbanken said.
The outlook for Finnish government bonds remained positive.
"Improving fundamentals coupled with the ERM and EMU situation suggest a diminishing interest rate differential," Handelsbanken said.
In early trade on Wednesday, the yield gap between Finland's new 10-year benchmark and German bunds narrowed to a historical low of 57 basis points.
